items.prompt: Which term describes repeating back, in your own words, what the other person said to confirm you understood it?

options.label: Escalating
Paraphrasing
Deflecting
Arbitrating

rubric: Paraphrasing restates the speaker's message to check understanding.
Arbitrating is a third party imposing a decision, not a listening skill.

items.prompt: In conflict resolution, what is a person's 'interest'?

options.label: The deadline they set for a decision
The rule they cite to support their view
The exact demand they state at the start
The underlying need or concern behind what they ask for

rubric: An interest is the underlying need or concern behind a demand.
The stated demand is a position, which is commonly confused with an interest.

items.prompt: What is the role of a mediator in a dispute?

options.label: To support whichever party is weaker
To report the dispute to senior management
To decide who is right and impose a ruling
To help the parties reach their own agreement

rubric: A mediator is neutral and facilitates; the parties decide the outcome.
Imposing a ruling describes arbitration or a judge.

items.prompt: Which phrase is an example of an 'I' statement?

options.label: Everyone knows you are careless about time
Your lateness shows you do not care
I feel frustrated when meetings start late
You always show up late to meetings

rubric: An 'I' statement describes your own feeling and the behaviour without blaming.
The other options begin with 'you' or generalise, which is accusatory.

items.prompt: Which is a de-escalation technique when someone is shouting?

options.label: Interrupting to correct their facts
Speaking calmly and at a lower volume
Matching their volume to show you are serious
Telling them to calm down immediately

rubric: Calm, lower-volume speech helps lower tension.
Matching volume or ordering calm usually escalates things.

items.prompt: Which are active listening behaviours? Select all that apply.

options.label: Asking open questions to clarify
Preparing your rebuttal while they talk
Finishing their sentences for them
Maintaining appropriate eye contact

rubric: Eye contact and clarifying questions show attention to the speaker.
Planning a rebuttal or finishing sentences means you are not truly listening.

items.prompt: Two colleagues keep arguing over who owns a task. They agree to ask a neutral third person to help them talk it through, but the third person will not decide for them. Which process is this?

options.label: Arbitration
Litigation
Mediation
Avoidance

rubric: A neutral helper who doesn't decide is a mediator.
Arbitration involves a binding decision by the third party.

items.prompt: Why is it useful to focus on interests rather than positions?

options.label: Positions are always dishonest
Different positions can often satisfy the same underlying needs
It lets one side win more quickly
Interests are easier to ignore

rubric: Looking at interests opens up options that meet both sides' needs.
Positions are not dishonest; they are just narrow ways to meet a need.

items.prompt: Why does active listening help reduce conflict?

options.label: It proves the listener is right
It lets the listener avoid speaking at all
It forces the other person to stop talking
People who feel heard are less defensive and more open

rubric: Feeling understood lowers defensiveness.
Listening is not about winning or silencing.

items.prompt: Which best explains why a 'win-win' outcome is usually preferred to compromise by splitting the difference?

options.label: It is always faster to reach
It avoids any discussion of needs
It guarantees both sides get everything they asked for
It meets both sides' real needs, so the agreement lasts

rubric: Win-win addresses underlying needs, so it tends to hold.
It does not guarantee everything requested or skip discussion.

items.prompt: Which statement is the best reframe of 'You never listen to my ideas'?

options.label: You are a bad listener
Nobody here wants ideas
I'd like my ideas to be considered before we decide
Stop ignoring me

rubric: Reframing turns blame into a stated need and request.
The others keep or increase the blame.

items.prompt: Which of these is a conflict about a value rather than about a resource?

options.label: Two teams both want the same meeting room
Two teammates disagree on whether honesty matters more than loyalty
Two managers share one limited budget
Two staff want the same holiday dates

rubric: Honesty versus loyalty is a clash of beliefs or values.
The others are disputes over scarce resources.

items.prompt: Which are common causes of workplace conflict? Select all that apply.

options.label: Competition for limited resources
Having a shared, clearly agreed goal
Clear and timely communication
Unclear roles and responsibilities

rubric: Role ambiguity and scarce resources commonly spark disputes.
Shared goals and clear communication tend to reduce conflict.

items.prompt: Sam tells a coworker, 'I'm not working with you again.' The coworker replies, 'It sounds like you're upset about how the deadline was handled. Is that right?' What is the coworker doing and why does it help?

options.label: Reflecting the feeling to check understanding and lower tension
Making a demand so Sam must respond
Changing the subject to avoid conflict
Agreeing to blame themselves to end the talk

rubric: Reflecting feeling and checking shows understanding and calms the exchange.
It is not an apology, avoidance or a demand.

items.prompt: In conflict resolution, what is the difference between a person's position and their interest?

options.label: A position is the firm demand stated aloud, and an interest is the underlying need behind it
A position is the emotion shown in the dispute, and an interest is the fact being argued
A position is the rule that applies, and an interest is the person's preferred outcome
A position is the compromise someone will accept, and an interest is the demand they open with

rubric: Interests are the needs, worries or goals behind a stated demand (position).
Distractors mix up demand, compromise and emotion with interest.

items.prompt: Why does an active listener paraphrase what the other person has said during a disagreement?

options.label: To check understanding and show the speaker they were heard
To signal agreement so the speaker will stop arguing
To steer the speaker toward the listener's conclusion
To buy time to prepare a stronger counterargument

rubric: Paraphrasing confirms accuracy and shows the speaker they were understood.
Distractors treat it as a tactic or as agreement, which it is not.

items.prompt: Two teammates disagree about launching on Friday because one has not seen the latest test results the other has. What type of conflict is this mainly?

options.label: A power conflict
A relationship conflict
A values conflict
An information conflict

rubric: The disagreement stems from unequal or missing information, so sharing data should help.
Values or relationship labels are tempting but nothing in the case shows them.

items.prompt: Why is it usually wise to de-escalate strong emotions before starting to problem-solve?

options.label: Because strong emotions prove that one side is mistaken on the facts
Because high emotion narrows thinking, making it hard to weigh options fairly
Because the person who calms down first has effectively won the dispute
Because problem-solving only works once both sides have agreed on who is to blame

rubric: Intense emotion limits listening and flexible thinking, so calming comes first.
Distractors treat calming as winning, as proof of error, or as needing blame settled.

items.prompt: A manager hears one employee's side of a dispute and immediately rules in that person's favour without hearing the other. What is the most likely result?

options.label: The other employee gains trust in the manager's fairness
The dispute ends quickly because the authority has spoken
The other employee feels unheard, and resentment is likely to continue
Both employees accept the outcome because it was fast

rubric: Skipping one party's account leaves them feeling unheard and fuels hidden resentment.
Distractors assume that speed or authority creates acceptance.

items.prompt: Which of the following are signs that a conflict is escalating? Select all that apply.

options.label: The discussion shifts from the issue to personal attacks
Each side starts recruiting colleagues to take their side
One person asks a question to clarify the other's concern
People use words like "always" and "never" about each other

rubric: Personal attacks, absolute language and recruiting allies are classic escalation signs.
Clarifying questions tend to reduce escalation.

items.prompt: Priya and Sam wrote a report together. In the team meeting, Sam presented it as his own work, and afterwards Priya snapped, "You always take the credit!" Sam became defensive. What does Priya's outburst most likely signal about her underlying interest?

options.label: She wants the report deadline to be extended
She wants Sam removed from the project
She wants to win the argument in front of the team
She wants her contribution to be acknowledged

rubric: The accusation about credit points to a need for recognition.
Distractors treat the angry words as the real goal rather than a signal of the interest.

items.prompt: A colleague keeps interrupting you in meetings. Which statement is a well-formed I-statement to open the conversation?

options.label: "I feel that you are rude and never let anyone speak."
"I think you should stop interrupting me in meetings."
"I feel like you interrupt because you don't respect me."
"I feel cut off when I'm interrupted, and I'd like to finish my point first."

rubric: A good I-statement names a feeling, the behaviour and a request, without blaming or guessing motives.
Distractors disguise accusations or commands as I-statements.

items.prompt: A coworker says, "I'm sick of covering for Jo's late handoffs; my evenings are gone." Which reply best applies active listening?

options.label: "Jo is probably just overloaded, so try being more patient."
"Everyone gets frustrated with late handoffs sometimes."
"So Jo's late handoffs push your work into evenings, and it's wearing you down?"
"Have you thought about taking this to Jo's manager?"

rubric: Reflecting content and feeling in your own words is active listening.
Distractors defend Jo, jump to advice, or minimise the feeling.

items.prompt: Two departments each demand the only shared laptop cart on Monday mornings. Using an interest-based approach, what should you do next?

options.label: Ask each department what it needs the laptops for and when
Alternate the cart weekly between the two departments
Let the department with the more senior leader take it
Split the cart so each department gets half the laptops

rubric: Exploring each side's underlying needs comes before proposing solutions.
Distractors jump to splitting, rank or rotation without learning the interests.

items.prompt: A customer is shouting at you at the service desk about a billing error. Which first response best applies de-escalation?

options.label: Tell the customer firmly to calm down before you can help
Raise your voice slightly so you can be heard over them
Speak calmly, let them finish, and acknowledge their frustration
Explain the billing policy right away so the facts are clear

rubric: Staying calm, letting the person vent and acknowledging feeling lowers tension.
Distractors invalidate emotions, argue facts too early, or match the volume.

items.prompt: You are mediating between two coworkers. You have explained your role and set ground rules. Which step comes next in a typical mediation?

options.label: Have both parties sign a written agreement
Propose a settlement for both parties to accept
Invite each party to tell their story without interruption
Meet each party privately and decide who is at fault

rubric: After the opening and ground rules, each party gets uninterrupted time to explain.
Distractors jump ahead to solutions, signing or judging.

items.prompt: You need to raise a recurring problem with a coworker in a one-on-one conversation. Which actions apply good practice? Select all that apply.

options.label: Invite their view and listen before suggesting solutions
Open by summing up all their past mistakes
Choose a private time when neither of you is rushed
Describe the specific behaviour and its effect on you

rubric: Privacy, specific behaviour-impact description and inviting their view keep the talk constructive.
Listing past mistakes feels like an attack and raises defensiveness.

items.prompt: You mediate between Marcus and Lena. Lena says Marcus changes plans at the last minute. Marcus says Lena never tells him the team's priorities. Both want to stay on the project. Which agreement best addresses both interests?

options.label: The manager reassigns one of them to another project
Marcus agrees to stop changing plans without exception
A weekly priorities check-in, with plan changes flagged the day before
Lena emails Marcus daily and he confirms every message

rubric: The check-in gives Marcus visibility and gives Lena advance notice, so it meets both interests.
Distractors meet only one side's interest or remove the problem rather than resolving it.

items.prompt: Two coordinators each insist, "I must have the boardroom at 2pm Thursday." You want to move them from positions to interests. Which question do you ask next?

options.label: Why is your need for the room more urgent than your colleague's?
What would having the room at that time let each of you achieve?
Who booked the room first, and can that be checked in the system?
Could one of you simply take the 3pm slot to keep things fair?

rubric: Asking what the slot lets each person achieve surfaces underlying interests that may allow other solutions.
Distractors stay with positions: precedence, splitting the difference, or competing urgency.

items.prompt: A teammate says angrily, "You keep changing the specs and then blaming us for the delays." Which reply best applies active listening?

options.label: I understand you're upset, but the client is the one who requested those spec changes.
Let's not point fingers; what matters is how we deliver from this point forward.
I hear that the spec changes are causing delays and that you feel blamed. Is that right?
That isn't accurate, since I've only changed the specs twice during this quarter.

rubric: Paraphrasing content and feeling, then checking accuracy, is the core active listening move.
Other options defend, deflect or dismiss before the person feels understood.

items.prompt: At a service desk, a customer begins shouting about a refused refund while other customers watch. What is the best first move?

options.label: Speak slowly and quietly, name their frustration, and offer to continue somewhere more private
Tell them firmly you can only help once they have calmed down and lowered their voice
Match their energy and pace, promising an immediate refund so the scene ends quickly
Explain the refund policy step by step so they see the decision is fair and consistent

rubric: De-escalation starts with a calm tone, acknowledging emotion and lowering the stakes of the setting.
Explaining policy or demanding calm too early escalates; matching energy and caving rewards the shouting.

items.prompt: A flatmate complains, "He never does his share of the cleaning." Which reframe turns this into an interest-based statement?

options.label: You think he is lazy and expects you to do everything.
You believe he should be penalised whenever he skips a chore.
You are saying the cleaning rota has never worked for anyone.
You want the flat to stay clean and the workload to feel fair.

rubric: Reframing names the underlying needs (cleanliness, fairness) without blame.
Distractors keep the blame, punishment or sweeping generalisation.

items.prompt: You are mediating a dispute between two employees. Introductions and ground rules are done. According to a standard mediation process, what comes next?

options.label: Both parties negotiate and sign a final written agreement right away
Each party gives an uninterrupted account of the situation and what they need
You state who seems to be at fault and propose terms to settle it
Both parties brainstorm and vote together on possible settlement options

rubric: After ground rules, each party tells their story uninterrupted so issues and interests can be identified.
The other options jump ahead to solutions, judgement or closure.

items.prompt: During a mediation you hold a private caucus with one party. Which uses of the caucus are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.label: Tell the party privately they are in the right so they stay engaged
Share confidential details the party disclosed with the other side to speed progress
Choose the final settlement and persuade the party to accept it
Let the party vent safely and clarify what they actually need from the outcome
Test how realistic a demand is without the other party hearing the discussion

rubric: Caucuses suit reality-testing and safe venting or clarifying needs while keeping confidentiality.
Breaching confidence, taking sides or imposing a settlement undermines mediator neutrality.

items.prompt: Two team leads, Mia and Raj, clash over who gets the one available developer next sprint. Mia cites a client deadline; Raj cites a security fix. Each has repeated their position twice. You are their manager acting as mediator. What should you do next?

options.label: Have both restate their cases more concisely, then back whichever argument is stronger
Give the developer to the more senior lead to end the argument quickly
Split the developer's week evenly so both feel they were treated equally
Ask each to explain the consequences and constraints behind their request, then list shared goals

rubric: Exploring underlying consequences and shared goals moves the pair from positions to interests.
Even splitting, seniority or judging arguments ignore interests and may leave both unhappy.

items.prompt: A dispute about missed deadlines between design and engineering has been "settled" three times with new dates, yet it keeps recurring. Which underlying cause is most worth investigating?

options.label: Neither team has agreed who owns the handoff criteria, so each assumes the other is late
The new deadlines were not set tightly enough to motivate either team to hurry
The teams have not had enough social contact to build trust between themselves
One individual is personally difficult and provokes the conflict again each round

rubric: A recurring dispute after repeated date fixes points to a structural cause such as unclear ownership of handoffs.
The distractors blame motivation, personality or trust without evidence from the pattern.

items.prompt: Two departments split a disputed budget 50/50. Both left resentful and the issue returned a month later. Which analysis best explains this?

options.label: Compromise is always inferior to a clear win-lose decision and should be avoided
The split divided positions without exploring interests, so neither core need was fully met
The split should have favoured the more senior department to be accepted
The departments needed longer to vent their feelings before agreeing on numbers

rubric: Splitting the difference without exploring interests often leaves underlying needs unmet.
Other options overgeneralise about compromise, rely on seniority or misdiagnose the missing step.

items.prompt: Ten minutes into a mediation, the mediator says, "It sounds like you just need a weekly check-in. Shall we agree to that?" Both parties go quiet and reluctantly nod. What is the main flaw?

options.label: A solution was proposed before interests were surfaced, so the agreement is shallow
The mediator should have met each party privately before the session began
Check-ins are an ineffective remedy for communication problems between colleagues
The mediator skipped ground rules, so the parties felt unable to disagree

rubric: Proposing a fix before exploring interests yields reluctant, fragile agreement.
Other options name process steps or claims that the scenario does not support.

items.prompt: An email thread starts with "The report is missing," then "You always do this," then "Typical of your department," and ends with the manager copied in. Which dynamic best describes the escalation?

options.label: A factual disagreement that more data would settle between the two people
An accommodating style that avoids confronting the real issue directly
A shift from the specific issue to character and group attributions, widening the conflict
Healthy assertiveness that clarifies the stakes for everyone involved

rubric: Moving from a specific event to "always" and group labels signals personalising and widening the conflict.
The distractors mislabel the pattern as assertiveness, accommodation or a factual dispute.

items.prompt: A buyer asked a supplier for a 10% discount. The supplier offered 10% off the next order, and the buyer refused. Later it emerged that the buyer's manager needs visible savings this quarter. Why was the offer rejected?

options.label: Ten percent was simply too small, and a larger discount would have been accepted
The buyer was bargaining in bad faith and never intended to accept any offer
The buyer needed more time to feel heard before any offer could be considered
The offer matched the stated position but not the hidden interest in savings this quarter

rubric: The offer met the stated position but missed the timing interest behind it.
Distractors assume bad faith, price alone or an unsupported need to be heard.

items.prompt: Which observations suggest a conflict is mainly relational rather than task-based? Select all that apply.

options.label: The parties argue about tone and past slights more than about the work
The disagreement persists even after the facts and the plan are agreed
The parties share goals but differ over which software tool to adopt
A new data report resolved most of the disagreement between them
Each party readily accepts the other's proposed changes to the task

rubric: Persistence after task issues are settled, and a focus on tone and past slights, point to relational conflict.
The other observations describe task disagreements that data or flexibility can resolve.

items.prompt: In mediation, Dana and Lee agreed Lee would send updates by Friday noon. Within a week Lee missed it twice and Dana is furious. Lee now says the deadline was impossible because the data arrives at 1pm, but he said nothing in the session. Which analysis best explains the breakdown?

options.label: Written agreements are unnecessary, since trust matters more than a documented deadline
Lee is deliberately breaking the agreement to retaliate against Dana
The agreement was never tested for feasibility, and Lee's silence suggests concerns that went unsurfaced
Dana's expectation was reasonable, so only Lee needs to change his behaviour

rubric: The agreement skipped a feasibility check, and Lee's silence suggests unspoken constraints or face concerns.
Other options assume malice, dismiss documentation or blame one party without evidence.

items.prompt: A project manager notices that three different analysts have each clashed with the same account director over report formats in the past year. Which inference does this pattern best support?

options.label: The analysts lack the skills to follow clear instructions
The cause is likely structural, such as unclear format ownership
Each clash is an unrelated personality mismatch to handle alone
The account director is deliberately targeting analysts

rubric: A repeated pattern across different people points to a shared structural cause like unclear ownership or process.
Distractors jump to blaming individuals or treating each clash as isolated.

items.prompt: In a mediation, a party grows louder each time the mediator paraphrases their account, even though the paraphrase is factually accurate. What is the most likely cause?

options.label: Paraphrasing always raises tension and should be avoided entirely
The party disputes the facts and wants them restated word for word
The paraphrase captured the facts but missed the concern behind them
The party is using volume to gain leverage over the other side

rubric: Accurate content with missed emotion or underlying concern leaves the person feeling unheard, so they escalate.
Distractors assume manipulation or reject paraphrasing rather than diagnosing the mismatch.

items.prompt: Sam tells a colleague, "You always miss deadlines, and it shows you don't care." The colleague snaps back and the talk collapses. Which element most directly caused the escalation?

options.label: Attributing a character flaw through a sweeping generalisation
Failing to schedule the discussion at a more formal time
Raising the topic of deadlines in a direct conversation
Expressing frustration at all instead of staying neutral

rubric: Global words like 'always' plus a motive attribution attack identity and trigger defensiveness.
Distractors blame the topic, timing or emotion, which are not the main trigger.

items.prompt: Two peers publicly agree to a new handover process, then both quietly keep using their old methods. Which diagnosis best fits?

options.label: The manager failed to state the penalties for noncompliance
The meeting was too short for the process to be explained
Both peers are unwilling to accept any change from anyone
Agreement stayed at the position level, leaving interests unspoken

rubric: Surface agreement without surfacing underlying interests produces compliance in the room but no real commitment.
Distractors blame stubbornness, time or enforcement rather than the unexamined interests.

items.prompt: Which statement from a supplier in a delivery dispute most clearly expresses an interest rather than a position?

options.label: "Our contract says the 12th, so the 12th is what you get."
"We will not deliver any earlier than the 12th."
"Your demand for the 10th is simply unreasonable for us."
"We need the 12th because our packing line is shared that week."

rubric: An interest states the underlying need or constraint; the others restate a fixed demand or appeal to a rule.
Distractors are positions, even when they sound reasoned.

items.prompt: A disagreement over a design review began as a task dispute. Which observations suggest it has shifted into a relationship conflict? Select all that apply.

options.label: Each person now avoids the other and routes messages through third parties
Participants ask for the review criteria to be clarified
Both sides still cite evidence about the design itself
Comments now target each other's competence and motives
Side conversations recast earlier disagreements as proof of bad faith

rubric: Personal attacks, avoidance and reinterpreting the past as bad faith show the conflict is now about the people.
Citing design evidence and clarifying criteria remain task-focused.

items.prompt: After a production outage, a mediator meets the operations lead and the developer privately. The ops lead says the developer "never listens to alerts." The developer says ops "always hunts for someone to blame." In private each admits fearing being named responsible in the incident report. What should the mediator conclude about the driver of the conflict?

options.label: The incident report is poorly designed and should be rewritten
One party is lying and the facts must be verified first
Each fears blame, so the dispute is really about protecting standing
The two have incompatible working styles that need coaching

rubric: The shared private fear of blame is the interest driving their accusations, so any solution must address it.
Distractors treat symptoms (styles, document format) or assume dishonesty.

items.prompt: Two team members who share a desk pod and must collaborate daily have a recurring friction. Criteria: preserve the working relationship, resolve it within a week, and keep the outcome owned by them. Which approach best meets these?

options.label: A facilitated joint conversation where they agree their own working norms
Moving one of them to another team to remove contact
A manager's written ruling that sets the rules for both
Separate coaching sessions with no joint discussion

rubric: A facilitated joint conversation is quick, keeps the relationship and gives them ownership.
Distractors impose a decision, avoid the conflict or skip the other party.

items.prompt: In a mediation, one party is visibly flooded with anger and cannot listen to the other. Criteria: protect the other party, keep the process viable, and avoid hardening positions. What is the best next step?

options.label: Ask the angry party to apologise before moving forward
Hold a private caucus with the angry party to settle them first
Continue the joint session so both sides hear everything
End the mediation and recommend formal arbitration

rubric: A caucus lets the person de-escalate and be heard without damaging the joint process.
Distractors push on with a flooded party, demand concessions early, or abandon the process.

items.prompt: A customer is shouting about a faulty order. Criteria: lower the emotional temperature, learn what outcome the customer wants, and stay within policy. Which opening is best?

options.label: Offer a full refund at once to end the confrontation
Name the specific frustration, then ask what outcome they want
Ask the customer to calm down before you can continue
Quote the refund policy so expectations are clear immediately

rubric: Naming the specific frustration de-escalates and the question surfaces the desired outcome within policy.
Distractors invalidate feelings, lead with rules, or concede before understanding the need.

items.prompt: Two departments each ask for the full training budget. A director splits it 50/50 as "fair" without asking why each needs it. Which critique is most valid?

options.label: Even splits always cause resentment and should never be used
It ignores underlying needs, so both may be left unable to meet them
Splitting is unfair because the larger department should get more
The director should have deferred the decision to a vote

rubric: A split made without exploring interests can leave both needs unmet where a better trade might exist.
Distractors assert fixed fairness rules or blanket claims rather than critiquing the missing interest exploration.

items.prompt: A mediated agreement must hold for six months. Which risk should be ranked highest for durability?

options.label: The parties did not shake hands at the end of the session
One party signed because they felt pressured to end the session
The agreement is a page shorter than similar past agreements
The follow-up check-in is booked a week later than planned

rubric: Coerced consent undermines commitment and is the top threat to long-term durability.
Other options are minor procedural or cosmetic points.

items.prompt: A manager wants to judge whether a settled dispute was resolved well. Which criteria are sound? Select all that apply.

options.label: A follow-up check is set to review how it is working
The meeting finished faster than usual
The loudest party reports being satisfied
The underlying interests of both parties are addressed
Each party can restate their commitments in their own words

rubric: Shared understanding, addressed interests and follow-up predict a durable resolution.
Satisfaction of one side and speed say little about quality.

items.prompt: Two skilled engineers disagree on an architecture choice and a decision is due in two days. Each is firm, and both are respected. The lead must pick a process. Criteria: decision quality, speed, and both staying engaged afterwards. Which approach is best?

options.label: Agree decision criteria with both, then decide against them openly
Hold a team vote so the majority view decides quickly
Blend both designs into a hybrid so neither side loses
Defer to the more senior engineer to avoid a lengthy debate

rubric: Agreed criteria make the decision transparent and merit-based, supporting engagement even for the person who loses.
Distractors trade quality for speed or avoid the actual trade-off.

items.prompt: A trainer teaches 'separate the people from the problem' as a universal rule. In which situation does the rule fit worst?

options.label: A customer and an agent dispute a refund policy and the customer is visibly frustrated
Two departments argue over budget because each fears losing headcount to the other
A colleague keeps belittling teammates in meetings, so the behaviour itself is the problem
Two engineers disagree on a database choice and each feels their expertise was ignored

rubric: When a person's conduct is the issue, it cannot be separated from the person; it has to be addressed directly.
The other options have relationship strain, but the substantive problem is still separable.

items.prompt: Two long-term business partners want to keep working together and are disputing roles. Criteria: preserve the relationship, use their own deep business knowledge, and give them ownership of the outcome. Which mediation style fits best?

options.label: Evaluative, where the mediator judges the merits and proposes a settlement range
Binding arbitration, where a neutral issues a final decision that both must follow
Directive, where the mediator sets the terms and then monitors compliance closely
Facilitative, where the mediator manages the process and the partners build their own terms

rubric: Facilitative mediation keeps ownership with the parties and protects the relationship.
Evaluative, directive and arbitral approaches move the decision to a third party, which suits cases needing legal or rights-based outcomes.

items.prompt: An employee says her director takes credit for her work, and she fears retaliation. HR offers mediation. Judging by safety and fairness, what is the best first step?

options.label: Open with a joint session so both hear the same account together and nobody suspects side deals
Run joint mediation with strictly equal speaking time, since equal treatment guarantees fairness
Ask her to raise it informally with the director first so formal processes remain a last resort
Hold separate private sessions first to check voluntariness and safety and agree protections before any joint meeting

rubric: With a power gap and fear of retaliation, private screening and safeguards must come before a joint session.
Equal airtime does not offset structural power; informal self-advocacy puts the risk on the weaker party.

items.prompt: Two product managers split a quarter's resources 50/50 after a dispute and both are unhappy. One cares mainly about launch date, the other about feature scope. How should you critique this compromise?

options.label: It is sound, because any quickly reached agreement lowers the cost of the conflict
It is sound, because equal concessions are the most legitimate basis for fairness
It is flawed mainly because it was imposed rather than put to a vote by the wider team
It leaves value on the table, since trading on the issue each values more could leave both better off than an even split

rubric: Different priorities allow logrolling, which creates joint gain that a split-the-difference deal misses.
Equal splits feel fair but are often inefficient; speed and voting do not address the lost value.

items.prompt: A mediator under time pressure pushes two parties to sign an agreement while they are still arguing fixed positions on a payment amount. What is the most serious risk of this approach?

options.label: The deal settles positions but not underlying interests, so it tends to be brittle and the dispute re-emerges
The agreement is signed only for the sake of ending the session, so it is cheaper to document later
The parties may resent the mediator for pushing and refuse to use mediation again
The deal may be too generous to whichever side argued more forcefully in the session

rubric: Position-level deals leave the drivers of the conflict untouched, so they often fail or recur.
Resentment and generosity are possible but secondary risks.

items.prompt: You are judging whether a negotiated settlement between two managers is likely to last. Which criteria are sound evidence of durability? Select all that apply.

options.label: Both signed during the same meeting where the dispute peaked in intensity
The agreement contains a specific check-in date and a way to handle breaches
Both sides felt heard and saw the process as fair, even where they gave ground
The mediator privately rated the outcome as fair to both parties
Each side's core interests are visibly met, not only their stated positions

rubric: Durable agreements meet interests, are seen as procedurally fair, and have follow-up mechanisms.
Signing at peak emotion and the mediator's opinion say little about whether the parties will comply.

items.prompt: Two team leads dispute who gets a shared specialist for the next two weeks, and each accuses the other of hoarding. A release is due in 48 hours, and they must still collaborate next quarter. You manage both and must choose a response that meets the deadline and protects the relationship.

options.label: Give the specialist to the lead with the higher-priority project and keep your reasoning private to avoid debate
Decide now using criteria you state openly, then schedule a later session on how to share scarce resources
Wait until they reach consensus, because imposed decisions always damage trust
Split the specialist's time 50/50 so neither can claim the other was favoured

rubric: The deadline justifies a decision, but transparent criteria and a follow-up session protect procedural fairness and the relationship.
Waiting misses the deadline, an even split ignores need, and a private rationale breeds suspicion.

items.prompt: You must design the opening of a mediation between two teams blaming each other for a failed launch. It must establish neutrality, avoid a blame spiral, and keep focus on the future. Which design meets all three?

options.label: Say both teams share blame equally so nobody feels singled out, then ask for improvement ideas
Begin with a trust exercise to rebuild goodwill, and take up the launch only in a later session
Have each team list the failures in order so the facts are agreed before any talk of solutions
Explain the process and confidentiality, ask each side for the impact and what they need going forward, and park fault-finding

rubric: It sets neutral ground rules and redirects from fault to needs and future.
Fact-listing feeds blame, pre-judging shared fault undermines neutrality, and avoiding the issue delays resolution.

items.prompt: Sales and operations clash weekly over custom orders. Design a fix that reduces recurrence, avoids daily escalations to executives, and keeps each function accountable for its own targets. Which is best?

options.label: Train both teams in active listening and rely on goodwill to resolve each order case by case
Define decision criteria and decision rights for custom orders, with a fast-track review and a named tiebreaker
Give operations the final say on every custom order, since it carries the capacity risk
Hold a weekly meeting of both heads to discuss every disputed order and agree on it jointly

rubric: Clear criteria and decision rights address the structural cause while keeping accountability.
The other options keep escalations, shift accountability to one side, or ignore the structure.

items.prompt: A mediated agreement between two coworkers says only that each will 'communicate respectfully' and 'share information promptly.' What is the most important thing it is missing?

options.label: Observable behaviours and a check-in with a defined way to handle breaches, so terms can be tested
A formal apology from the coworker seen as more at fault, to restore the other's dignity
A confidentiality clause forbidding either person from describing the dispute to colleagues
A neutral third party who will decide which coworker is right if the dispute recurs

rubric: Vague terms cannot be verified; specific behaviours plus review and breach handling make an agreement workable.
Apologies, confidentiality and a judge do not fix unmeasurable commitments.

items.prompt: A client says 'I will not accept any delay.' You must reply in a way that surfaces their interest, does not concede, and does not challenge their position. Which reply meets all three?

options.label: 'That date clearly matters; what happens for you if delivery lands after it, and what would make a later date workable?'
'Deadlines are rarely fixed, so which part of the project could you give up to keep it?'
'I understand, but a delay is unavoidable, so what can we do to make you comfortable?'
'I will promise the original date and we will sort out any problems on our side afterwards.'

rubric: It acknowledges the position, probes the interest behind it, and invites options without conceding.
The other replies concede falsely, challenge the position, or announce the bad news without inquiry.

items.prompt: On a three-person team, two members consistently align against the third, who has gone quiet. Design an intervention that gives the third member voice, avoids a public confrontation, and addresses the issues rather than the alliance. Which is best?

options.label: Meet each person individually to learn their interests, then run a structured joint session by issue with turn-taking rules
Move the quiet member to another team so the conflict ends and the alliance can be left alone
Ask the two allied members to apologise publicly and then continue as before
Hold a team meeting where each person states who they think is causing problems

rubric: Individual conversations protect the quiet member, and structured issue-based turns keep the focus off the alliance.
Public attribution, relocation and public apologies fail one or more constraints.

items.prompt: You are writing a conflict protocol for a remote team that mostly uses text chat, where misreadings keep escalating. Which elements would help it meet that need? Select all that apply.

options.label: Switch to live voice or video after two unresolved text exchanges
A named neutral contact whom either person can approach for help
A norm to ask a clarifying question before replying to a message that feels hostile
A ban on disagreement in public channels so conflicts stay hidden
A rule that any offence must be apologised for in writing within 24 hours

rubric: Moving to richer channels, clarifying intent and offering a neutral contact address text-driven escalation.
Banning disagreement and forced apologies suppress conflict rather than resolve it.

items.prompt: Two cofounders disagree on company direction and equity. One refuses a face-to-face meeting, both want confidentiality from investors, and a board update is in three weeks. As the mediator you must design a process that meets these constraints and can produce an outcome both accept.

options.label: Ask the advisory board to vote on the direction so neither founder has to concede to the other
Hold private caucuses to surface interests and test options, then run one short joint session on an agreed agenda and record an interim agreement
Postpone any process until after the board update, when pressure has eased
Put both in a joint meeting immediately with a lawyer present so legal rights are clear

rubric: Shuttle caucuses suit one founder's refusal to meet and keep things confidential, while a later joint session and written interim deal fit the deadline.
A forced joint meeting, a vote and delay each break at least one constraint.
